background_notes.fact: For a C¹ curve v:I→R^m on an open real interval, (v·v)'=2v·v'. In the Euclidean norm v·v=|v|²; hence |v|=1 throughout I implies v·v'=0 throughout I.

grounds.reason: Joint smoothness gives a C¹ time slice r↦u(x,r).
The slice has unit norm at every r>0.
t>0 is an interior point of the time interval.
The norm and dot product are Euclidean.

background_notes.justification: Write v·v=Σ_k v_k². Differentiating the finite sum by the scalar product rule gives Σ_k 2v_k v'_k=2v·v'. The derivative of the constant squared norm 1 is zero; division by 2 gives the identity.

background_notes.fact: For a C² curve v:I→R^m on an open interval, (v·v)''=2|v'|²+2v·v''. For a smooth map on R^n×(0,∞), this applies along time and each spatial coordinate line, with v',v'' equal to the corresponding classical partial derivatives. If the map has unit norm, u·u_tt=−|u_t|² and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|² at every point and every spatial index j.

grounds.reason: Joint C∞ regularity supplies C² time and spatial coordinate slices.
Unit norm holds identically along all these slices.
x is an arbitrary point of the full spatial domain.
Positive t allows a time interval around the point within the domain.
Classical partial derivatives and Euclidean norms have the stated meanings.

background_notes.justification: For each component differentiate v_k² twice: (v_k²)''=2(v'_k)²+2v_k v''_k. Sum over finitely many components. Restricting a smooth map to a coordinate line gives these one-variable derivatives by the definition of classical partial derivatives. Since v·v=1 along each slice, its second derivative vanishes, giving the two asserted identities.
